reports.title: Qatar 2026 — pre-weekend qualifying estimate
reports.html:
Qatar 2026 — pre-weekend qualifying estimate

Saved 24 November 2026, before any Qatar 2026 practice. Model B is the active forecast; A is the control; C is an experimental shadow. All three predict Kimi Antonelli fastest at 1:21.754 in a dry session. This is qualifying pace before race-grid penalties, with Q3-equivalent estimates for all 22 drivers, rather than separate Q1/Q2 elimination times.

Last year's qualifying

The official 2025 order began Piastri (1:19.387), Norris (1:19.495), Verstappen (1:19.651), Russell (1:19.662) and Antonelli (1:19.846). We retrieved the complete 20-driver Q1/Q2/Q3 classification, preserving each driver's 2025 team. Source: Formula 1 official 2025 Qatar qualifying.

Leclerc's Q3 was compromised by used tyres and a spin, so his recorded Q3 stays unchanged in the archive but his baseline uses a converted Q2 with a 0.50 context multiplier. Hamilton's Q1 exit supplies a lower-confidence converted baseline, without an invented incident correction. Team session accounts.

All 16 FIA deleted-lap entries are retained for audit. Faster deleted Q1/Q2 laps from Antonelli, Russell and Gasly do not replace their later valid Q3 times; out-laps, pit entries and slower deleted laps supply no pace reference. FIA deleted-lap record.

This week's scenario

Qualifying is Saturday 28 November, 21:00 Qatar / 18:00 UTC / 12:00 Chicago. This is a normal practice weekend; last year's Sprint format is not assumed. The initial scenario is dry, consistent with the current official preview, and must be revisited if conditions change. Official timetable, weekend preview.

Câmara replaces Ocon at Haas. His forecast uses the current Haas/team fallback; Ocon's personal 2025 Qatar lap is not assigned to him. Pérez's reported five-place race-grid penalty does not move his predicted qualifying position. Confirmed replacement and penalty context.

What the three models use

A: reliability-adjusted 60% historical same-track estimate and 40% aligned current-form estimate. Historical reliability r changes the effective historical share to 0.60r / (0.60r + 0.40). Without a personal historical baseline, current-form fallback supplies the prediction.

B: relative gaps from historical estimate, current team and current driver, with nominal weights 35% / 50% / 15%. Effective shares are 0.35r / (0.35r + 0.65), 0.50 / (0.35r + 0.65), and 0.15 / (0.35r + 0.65). Missing historical laps use 0% / 76.92% / 23.08%. The absolute pole anchor is the existing A-style anchor calculation, separate from the gap blend; it is not simply last year's pole plus one global year-on-year correction.

C: identical to B except the current-team signal receives a neutral-at-5 property correction relative to that team's reference circuit mix. k = 0.10 seconds per mile per confidence-weighted property point; the raw team correction is capped at ±0.10s, then sample-shrunk by n/(n+2), blended through B and recentered to B's pole anchor. Historical and driver signals stay fixed. Zero k reproduces B exactly. C is not validated for promotion.

Driver property scores already enter the existing historical estimate where available; C adds team properties rather than another driver bonus. Ratings assessed on 24 November are frozen unchanged: there has been no new 2026 qualifying since that assessment. Wet skills are untouched.

Current-form data and weights

The hierarchy is 50% latest-three form, 30% three most similar circuits, and 20% seven-event baseline. Latest-three weights within that component are 20% / 30% / 50% from oldest to newest. Combined base event weights are:

These are base weights, not identical contributions for every driver/team: lap reliability, Q1/Q2-to-Q3 conversion sample shrinkage, teammate coverage and upgrade regimes alter effective weights. Wet Brazil is excluded. Las Vegas is included with the previously recorded tow/context reliability reductions; it is not treated as uniformly clean evidence. Qatar 2026 practice has 0% weight at this cutoff.

Q3/Q2/Q1 nominal conversion reliability is 1.0/0.8/0.6, with additional conversion sample shrinkage and context multipliers. Clean direct Q3 baselines retain full historical reliability; converted or compromised baselines have smaller historical shares and low qualitative confidence.

What C changes at Qatar

Qatar's high-speed demand helps McLaren relative to its reference mix, while Ferrari's low-speed strength is less relevant here. C moves Verstappen ahead of Leclerc, and Norris narrowly ahead of Hadjar; it does not displace the Mercedes pair. The Norris–Hadjar separation is only about one millisecond, so that ordering is effectively a tie in practical terms.

Limits and evaluation plan

The common 1:21.754 pole estimate is 2.367s slower than Piastri's 2025 pole. That is the model's current cross-season pace projection, not a validated regulation or weather correction. Absolute timing remains less trustworthy than the relative comparison. Confidence labels are qualitative; no calibrated time intervals exist yet. Driver changes, year-to-year car changes, tyre preparation, traffic and track evolution can invalidate small predicted gaps.

After qualifying, preserve these forecasts and retrieve the official full stages and context first. Evaluate B, A and the separately saved C on the same driver population, recording gap error, position error and absolute-time error separately. Do not retune k or property scores with Qatar's result and then describe that same result as prospective validation. Practice can support a separately labelled update; no practice forecast is included here.

Saved evidence and revision

The published forecast is revision r2, frozen on 24 November. An unpublished preliminary snapshot mistakenly allowed faster deleted lower-stage laps to supersede clean valid Q3 laps. It is retained privately for audit and marked superseded; r2 excludes those lower-stage deleted laps from the baseline. No Qatar 2026 result was used in either version.

A/B have distinct locked IDs and C has its own pre_weekend_c shadow ID and artifact. The r2 manifest preserves the UTC lock time, source commit and code hashes, input hashes, dated rating copies, roster, team reference weights and frozen C settings. Forecast CSVs are the publication source; opening this website does not recalculate them.

reports.title: 2026 Las Vegas qualifying review
reports.html:
2026 Las Vegas qualifying review

Result and forecast integrity

Kimi Antonelli was fastest in 1:33.893, ahead of Max Verstappen (1:34.151), George Russell (1:34.224), Lando Norris and Isack Hadjar. Antonelli's penalty promoted Verstappen to the race pole; qualifying pace is evaluated before race-grid penalties. Bearman was officially not classified; the comparison uses last slot 22 for display, not an invented classified position.

Both locked forecasts were created on 16 November. They use the same current-form/property fallback because 2025 qualifying was wet, so their identical results are one model trial, not independent A/B evidence. No post-Friday forecast was created: FP1 had no timed benchmark and FP2 was wet. No hindsight Friday or FP3 forecast is substituted. Historical predictions are unchanged. The previously discussed wet-score adjustments remain unapplied.

Sources: F1 classification, FIA final classification, F1 session report.

Forecast performance

  • All-slot position MAE: 2.455, including Bearman's NC-as-last-slot proxy.
  • Context-filtered position MAE: 2.000, across 19 drivers; Hamilton, Câmara and Bearman are excluded for sourced compromised sessions.
  • Filtered rank correlation: 0.918.
  • Top-ten overlap: 8/10.
  • Q3 time MAE: 8.191s; Q3 relative-gap MAE: 0.391s.
  • Predicted pole anchor: 1:42.445, 8.552s slower than fastest qualifying.

The order was substantially more useful than the absolute times. The analogue anchor failed on the circuit's speed profile; the pre-weekend low-confidence warning did not make that error disappear. Do not tune driver ratings to fix an event-wide eight-second anchor error. The forecast selected Max for fastest qualifier, which was wrong even though he inherited race pole.

Neither model was better at Las Vegas. The missing dry 2025 baseline sent both through the same current-form/analogue fallback, bypassing their usual different historical-versus-current blends. This event tests that shared fallback; it cannot tell us whether A's or B's normal blend is superior.

Both captured much of the relative order but shared the large absolute-time anchor error. The filtered ranking excludes Hamilton, Câmara and Bearman for the same recorded reasons in both models; Q3 timing/gap metrics retain achieved tow-assisted laps. Do not compare one model's filtered score with the other's full-field score or count these identical forecasts as independent successes. A broader set of genuinely different locked A/B forecasts is needed to choose between their normal formulas.

How to weight the tows

Keep official times and classification unchanged. Both Antonelli and Verstappen had confirmed tow assistance on their best Q3 efforts. Their benefit was not quantified, so the 0.258s difference cannot establish a tow-free driver gap. Antonelli also described grip/braking difficulties; that does not justify subtracting an imagined tow gain or replacing his valid Q3 with his slower Q2.

For future pace learning, the following explicit reliability choices are now stored. They are conservative modelling judgements, not fitted probabilities or fractions of lap time attributable to a tow:

Base stage reliability is still Q3/Q2/Q1 = 1.0/0.8/0.6. For example, Hamilton's Q2 has effective reliability 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4. Kimi and Max's Q3 laps each retain 0.75. A weight of 0.75 does not add 25% to the lap time. Full/default weight for other drivers does not assert they drove in clean air; it reflects the available evidence. Missing a tow is not automatically a compromised lap, and a valid tow is not automatically invalid pace evidence.

Tow-assisted Q3 laps remain Q3 observations, rather than triggering the existing context-affected Q2 fallback. They do not define the shared Q1/Q2-to-Q3 stage-evolution estimate, because unequal tow opportunities distort conversion. Their compact-Q3 records have matching legacy weight overrides. The audit file data/las_vegas_2026_pace_context.csv records reasons. Official forecast metrics do not downweight Kimi or Max: a qualifying forecast must predict achieved laps.

Applying the same 0.75 to both is deliberately symmetric. We do not have enough evidence to assign Kimi 0.50 and Max 1.00, or to claim equal tow gains. Sensitivity checks at 0.50/0.75/1.00 should precede any coefficient tuning. No seconds are removed from either official lap, and driver wet skills are unchanged.

Sources: Antonelli interview, FIA session account confirming Verstappen's best-lap tow, team reports covering McLaren/Racing Bulls tows and compromised sessions.

What to learn next

The main structural failure was the same-track dry anchor being unavailable. Add a validated older-clean-lap or dry-practice anchor fallback, with explicit regulation/condition adjustments, rather than trusting seconds-per-mile scaling alone. Neither the older-baseline fallback nor an age multiplier is implemented.

Ferrari was forecast fourth/fifth but qualified 11th/12th; Hamilton's damage limits interpretation. Norris was underpredicted (seventh versus fourth), while Lindblad was 11th versus sixth. These misses justify examining circuit fit, tyre preparation and tow execution, not changing stable driver skill from one weekend. Keep model coefficients fixed until walk-forward comparisons support a change.

For towing, collect every representative lap's timing, sectors, compound, tyre age and gap to the car ahead along each straight. Compare runs at similar track conditions; sector deltas alone mix tow benefit with corner exits, deployment and tyre state. Separate team pace from teammate-relative evidence, since unequal tows can exaggerate teammate gaps. Current shared reliability weights are a temporary approximation to those separate effects.

This dry qualifying result is usable for future Vegas dry references with the recorded reliability. It must not calibrate wet FP2-to-dry-qualifying evolution; no clean FP2-to-pole calibration row was added.

reports.title: 2026 São Paulo qualifying review
reports.html:
2026 São Paulo qualifying review

Forecast provenance

The post-Friday dry forecast was reconstructed on 7 November 2026. FP1/FP2 classifications and Friday reports were retrieved first; the 22-driver forecast was saved before opening qualifying results. It is labelled locked_reconstructed, not a genuinely pre-session live forecast. Original pre-weekend snapshots remain unchanged. A search incidentally surfaced an FP3 snippet; no Saturday practice values were used. No coefficients were tuned against qualifying.

The pre-lookup copy is data/snapshots/brazil_2026_post_friday_before_qualifying_lookup.csv.

Friday inputs and decisions

All 22 entries from each Friday classification are stored, including guest FP1 drivers and Hülkenberg's untimed FP2 entry. Session gaps were converted to absolute seconds using each session's fastest lap. Guest laps were not assigned to the absent regular driver.

Leclerc's impeded soft run uses the existing weak-benchmark reliability of 0.25 (context_affected_no_clean_soft_lap); this is a model judgement, not an FIA classification change. His effective FP2 share is 10%, with unused weight returned to the prior. No speculative time correction was applied. Hülkenberg retains his prior with low confidence after missing Friday. Câmara inherits Ocon's car prior, uses his own Friday laps, and has low confidence as a debutant. No proxy lap from Ocon is used. Hamilton's setup/tyre difficulties alone do not establish an unusable best lap. Deleted FP2 laps were slower than valid benchmarks or pit-entry records, so none replaced a valid best.

Sources: FP1 classification, FP2 classification, Friday team reports, FP2 report, Haas driver change, FIA deleted FP2 laps.

Saved prediction and official result

The dry pole anchor was 1:09.241, subtracting the existing 1.522s calibrated gain from Antonelli's 1:10.763 FP2 best. The dry top five were Antonelli, Leclerc, Verstappen, Norris and Russell.

The filtered comparison excludes Verstappen (no Q2 attempt), Piastri (late red flag blocked improvement), Câmara (Q2 crash), Lindblad (ordered to stop), and Bortoleto (Q1 crash). It retains ordinary wet-condition outcomes. Pre-weekend snapshots did not include Câmara, so their matched-driver population differs from Friday; no synthetic pre-weekend forecast has been invented for him.

Interpretation and next work

Friday improved the ranking relative to Model B's pre-weekend forecast, but Model A still had the lower filtered position MAE. Friday's largest misses included Lawson (predicted 14th, qualified fifth), Alonso (16th versus ninth) and Albon (19th versus tenth). These are evidence that the dry ranking did not capture this wet session, rather than proof of a persistent dry team-pace shift.

Norris was fourth in the Friday dry order and won. Russell and Antonelli were also in the predicted top five. Leclerc's cautious reliability handling left him second rather than treating his impeded FP2 lap as fully representative; he qualified fourth. Hülkenberg's ninth-place prior forecast missed his sixth place, but Friday offered no direct lap evidence to justify a stronger update.

The forecast's dry pole was 18.229s faster than the wet actual pole. This is a condition mismatch and must not teach the dry anchor an 18-second correction. The previously stored wet/mixed simulation is experimental; it was not refit or regenerated after seeing this result. One event cannot calibrate its probabilities, and its pre-weekend roster does not represent Câmara's arrival.

Keep the 35/50/15 model coefficients unchanged. Next improvements should focus on weather-specific ranking evaluation, condition metadata, and honest replacement-driver uncertainty. Record comparable dry calibration events rather than adding Brazil to that sample.

reports.title: 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix qualifying review
reports.html:
2026 Mexico City Grand Prix qualifying review

Result

Lewis Hamilton took pole in 1:16.514, only 0.009s ahead of George Russell. Charles Leclerc, Max Verstappen, Kimi Antonelli, Lando Norris and Isack Hadjar completed the leading seven. All three forecasts selected exactly those seven drivers as the leading group, but none predicted Hamilton on pole.

Sources: official classification, FIA final classification, official team reports.

Three classifications require context:

  • Liam Lawson's original P8 time was removed when his car was disqualified for an MGU-K technical nonconformity. The breach occurred after the control line during the MGU-K step-down, and Racing Bulls argued that it produced no performance advantage. His 1:17.029 therefore remains future pace evidence at 50% reliability, while the disqualified position remains excluded from representative evaluation metrics.
  • Fernando Alonso was told to stop in Q1 with an ERS problem. His P17 is not representative pace.
  • Oliver Bearman's official Q2 best was 1:18.083, but his completed 1:17.847 was deleted for track limits. The deleted lap is stored separately at 35% confidence and his official classification is excluded from clean ranking metrics.

What worked

  • Model B improved the field order. Its top seven contained the exact seven actual front-runners, its top ten missed only Hülkenberg, and it had the best position MAE and rank correlation of the three forecasts.
  • Max's Friday gap was excellent. The model predicted P5 at +0.172s; he qualified P4 at +0.178s. This supports the strong Red Bull current-team signal used by Model B, even though his final attempt ended after a mistake at Turn 13.
  • The midfield boundary was mostly correct. Arvid and Pierre were predicted P10/P9 and finished P8/P9 after Lawson's disqualification. All forecasts had nine of the final top ten.
  • The absolute Friday anchor was useful. A 0.209s pole miss is much better than the common pre-weekend anchor, which was 1.199s too slow.

What missed and what we learned

1. Hamilton's interrupted FP2 was over-trusted. Model B had him P3, but the Friday blend moved him to P7 because his valid FP2 best was only P11 before a technical stoppage. He then found the correct tyre balance and took pole. Future technical-stop sessions should retain more of the pre-weekend prior, even when the driver's best lap itself remains valid. 2. Friday practice compressed the wrong drivers toward the front. Norris was predicted P2 and Piastri P8, but Norris qualified P6 and Piastri was eliminated in Q2. McLaren reported difficulty keeping the car in the same working window, while Piastri began Q2 on used tyres and did not execute his final lap. This is partly weekend execution rather than stable car pace. 3. The replacement-driver proxy was too optimistic. Hirakawa was predicted P12 but qualified P18. Using Ocon's FP2 car lap at 50% reliability was too strong for a driver making his qualifying debut. A future replacement proxy should be tested at 25% reliability or use the replacement's FP3 pace. 4. Model B should remain unchanged for now. It meaningfully improved field order over Model A, while Model A's relative-gap advantage was only 0.012s. Mexico does not support reducing the current-team weight after one test. 5. Deleted completed laps remain useful at low confidence. Bearman's deleted 1:17.847 was 0.236s faster than his valid Q2 best and is stored at 35% confidence. The other deleted completed laps were slower than valid stage bests or were obviously slow yellow-flag laps, so they receive zero model weight.

The main conclusion is that Model B improved the pre-weekend ranking, while Friday practice greatly improved absolute time but overreacted to incomplete or unrepresentative individual qualifying simulations. The next improvement should target session reliability, not the 35/50/15 Model B weights.

  • The pre-weekend model identified the exact six leading drivers as a group, showing that same-track history plus recent form remains useful for relative order even though the absolute times were slow.
  • Treating Hadjar's Friday as low confidence was correct. Setup changes made the car come alive in qualifying and he finished P3 rather than being punished for deleted Friday soft laps.
  • McLaren was correctly placed behind Mercedes, Red Bull and Ferrari. Piastri was predicted P8 and qualified P7; Norris's official P8 was affected by his deleted faster lap.

1. The post-Friday pole anchor was too aggressive. The model expected a 1.583s FP2-to-pole gain; the actual gain was 1.256s. Austin has been appended to the clean calibration dataset, which will reduce future bias. 2. Pre-weekend absolute pace was too slow. Clean-Q3 predictions missed by 1.089s despite good relative ordering. The year-over-year absolute-time transformation is less stable under the 2026 regulation change than the relative gaps. Future forecasts should expose separate confidence for absolute time and ranking. 3. Binary exclusion wastes useful Friday information. Carlos and Albon's deleted or non-comparable push laps were excluded, so Sainz fell back to an optimistic P9 despite Williams being slow throughout the weekend. A future session-evidence reliability field should allow a deleted but representative lap to enter at perhaps 25–50% weight instead of choosing between full weight and zero. 4. Overnight setup changes can beat the Friday prior. Mercedes and Hadjar improved materially on Saturday. The pre-weekend 5.412s time MAE is an absolute-anchor failure, not a failure of the whole ranking model. Sepang's era-adjusted 2017 anchor predicted a 1:30.221 pole, while the aggressive 2026 surface and conditions produced a 1:35.130. Its relative ordering still found nine of the ten Q3 drivers and achieved 0.811 rank correlation.

The headline post-Friday time MAE includes Gasly and Bortoleto's unrepresentative Q3 laps. Across the clean top eight it falls to 0.353s. After removing the common absolute offset and comparing gaps to Verstappen, the clean top-eight gap MAE is 0.265s.

What the result taught us

What worked

  • Max's medium-to-soft conversion was directionally correct. The model moved him from pre-weekend P6 to post-Friday P1, and he took pole.
  • Friday correctly identified Red Bull as a front-running car. Hadjar's actual P3 confirms that the signal was team-wide rather than a Verstappen-only lap.
  • The model found nine of the ten Q3 drivers at both stages. Most of the clean leading group was ranked closely even on a circuit absent since 2017.
  • The post-Friday forecast cut time MAE from 5.412s to 0.424s, showing why a real same-weekend anchor is essential at a new or long-absent circuit.

What failed

  • The generic median FP2-to-pole gain was 1.552s; the actual improvement from Leclerc's fastest FP2 lap to pole was 2.398s. That made most predicted Q3 times roughly 0.34s too slow on average across the clean top eight.
  • The model treated Russell and Antonelli's compromised FP2 soft laps mostly as driver uncertainty, but retained a very strong Mercedes prior. Mercedes then had its weakest Saturday of the year, and Russell fell to P8.
  • Hamilton's circuit familiarity was absent from the model. He and Verstappen were the only leading drivers with prior Sepang race experience; Hamilton's five previous poles were relevant on a track unfamiliar to most of the grid.
  • A deterministic top-ten list hides the very small midfield margins. Arvid was predicted P10 but used his penalty-affected session to tow Lawson, while Bortoleto reached Q3 after an Audi upgrade and strong execution.

Changes for future forecasts

1. Score relative pace separately from the absolute anchor. Publish a gap MAE and ranking score alongside time MAE. A single circuit-wide time offset should not make a useful ordering look like a complete model failure. 2. Use an anchor range, not only the historical median. Estimate the FP2-to-Q3 gain from comparable track-temperature, surface-evolution and tyre conditions, and publish at least a central estimate plus an uncertainty interval. Do not retune the median to this one event. 3. Shrink compromised driver laps toward a team practice estimate. Use timing data only to flag candidates: deleted laps, yellow/red flags, an unusually slow Q3 versus Q2, missing fresh-tyre runs, or an extreme teammate residual. Then verify the cause with official reports or team comments. Confirmed cases use the team estimate and reduced reliability; unexplained anomalies stay in the data with wider uncertainty rather than being silently removed. 4. Add a capped familiarity feature for returning circuits. Prior starts, representative qualifying laps and years since last use can contribute a small driver adjustment, capped near 0.10–0.15s and reduced after Friday. This must be backtested before it affects a live forecast. 5. Activate, but do not overfit, Red Bull's upgrade regime. Malaysia is the second usable team result since the Baku regime start. Model 2.7 can now use its specified 50/50 standard-versus-post-upgrade blend for the next race; it should not add a hand-tuned Sepang bonus. 6. Finish historical stage coverage before adding Q3 probabilities. The current sample is too small for calibrated advancement probabilities. First retrieve full Q1/Q2/Q3 classifications for the older races that still contain selected Q3 drivers only.

No broad team or driver property scores are changed from one result. The clean Malaysia laps are stored with full weight, Antonelli receives 0.7 because of his one-set Q3, and Gasly/Bortoleto receive 0.3 Q3-equivalent weights. Their official classification remains untouched in the factual result files.

What the Friday model got right

  • It predicted nine of the ten Q3 drivers. Colapinto was the only missed Q3 participant; Gasly was the incorrect selection.
  • Antonelli was predicted P1 and finished P2, only 0.011s from pole.
  • Hamilton and Piastri were predicted at their exact positions, P4 and P7.
  • Lawson was within one position despite being a substitute in the Red Bull.
  • Ocon, Sainz, and Alonso were also predicted at their exact final positions.
  • The FP2-based time recalibration reduced Q3 MAE by about 1.51s compared with the pre-weekend model.

What the Friday model got wrong

  • Norris was placed P5 because he set no FP2 time after completing only two laps. The per-driver normalization correctly avoided treating that as slow pace, but the remaining prior and FP1 evidence could not anticipate his exceptional final Q3 lap.
  • Verstappen was three places and 0.480s faster than forecast. His FP2 soft run showed strong pace, but long-run data was deliberately not allowed to alter a qualifying prediction.
  • Russell and Leclerc were each three positions too high. Friday headline times overstated their final ordering relative to Norris and Verstappen.
  • Colapinto was seven positions too low. His P15 FP2 classification was not representative of the pace he found through Q1, Q2, and Q3.
  • The absolute anchor remained conservative. Antonelli's 1:33.662 FP2 best improved by 1.838s to Norris's pole; the model assumed the recent median improvement of only 1.522s. That explains roughly 0.316s of the common positive Q3 time error.

The pre-weekend ranking was much better than its lap times suggest. It placed the eventual top seven drivers within its first seven active participants, predicted Piastri exactly P7, Lindblad exactly P10, and Bottas exactly P20 among classified drivers. Its 0.927 rank correlation was slightly better than the Friday model.

Its absolute time was unusable. The property-weighted historical analogue was 1:27.270, which pulled the published 1:32 design projection down to a 1:30.817 field anchor. Actual pole was 1:31.824. Property percentages and lap length did not capture Madring's real corner radii, surface grip, banking, or acceleration profile sufficiently well.

Model changes from Madrid

1. Preserve the hierarchical full-grid ranking approach; its broad ordering worked even before any car completed an F1 lap at Madrid. 2. For a new circuit, do not let a pace-per-mile analogue move the design or simulation projection by more than a declared cap until real laps exist. 3. After FP2, use an uncertainty range around the FP2-to-Q3 improvement rather than only its median. Madrid required 1.838s, 0.316s more than forecast. 4. Missing FP2 data should widen a driver's range rather than pulling the driver toward the centre. Norris demonstrated that no-time is uncertainty, not evidence of mediocre pace. 5. Add a session-progression feature. Colapinto improved sharply through the qualifying stages after an unrepresentative Friday. 6. Keep non-participation events separate from performance errors. Bearman's crash and Stroll's technical problem are not model pace failures.

The full stage result is stored in data/qualifying_stage_results.csv, the official comparable classification in data/actual_qualifying.csv, Q3 times in data/qualifying_results.csv, and materialized evaluation metrics in the prediction evaluation CSVs.

Archived Friday run analysis

OpenF1 session keys 11362 and 11363 supplied 1,042 lap records joined to compound, stint, and tyre age. The robust filter retained 83 clean laps across 14 runs of at least five laps. The most useful FP2 medium runs were Russell 1:39.611 over five clean laps, Antonelli 1:40.163 over five, Hamilton 1:40.568 over six, Bearman 1:41.432 over seven, Gasly 1:41.397 over seven, and Albon 1:42.287 over six. Verstappen averaged 1:39.952 across six clean laps on softs. These were stored as race-run evidence and did not alter the qualifying forecast because compounds, fuel, traffic, and run lengths differed.

2026 Monza qualifying review

Pierre Gasly took an unexpected maiden pole in 1:21.786, ahead of George Russell and Oscar Piastri. This was the model's largest failure: Gasly, Colapinto, and Lindblad were absent from the forecast because they lacked a usable previous-year Monza baseline, yet all three reached Q3. The result makes full-grid sparse-driver support a higher priority than further tuning among the already-modelled front-running drivers.

Verstappen's time was reasonably close, but the model placed him four positions too high because it missed Gasly, Piastri, and the front-running ordering around him.

This was intentionally an operational scenario rather than Antonelli's underlying pace prediction. It assumed he might provide a tow and then abort or set only a slow banker because his grid penalty removed the benefit of pole. That did not happen: he completed a Q3 time and classified P7. Consequently, the scenario had the worst time MAE (0.392s) and should not be used as the primary pace forecast. In future, grid penalties should create a separate strategy probability instead of replacing the main qualifying-time estimate.

Overall conclusions

  • Correct: Ferrari P4/P5 in the pre-weekend forecast, Russell close to the front, Verstappen P6 after Friday, and generally competitive absolute times for the established front-running drivers.
  • Partly correct: the partial-tow scenario correctly reversed the Mercedes order, but overestimated Antonelli's final Q3 execution.
  • Wrong: the model omitted three genuine Q3 drivers, placed Norris too high and Piastri too low, selected several drivers who did not reach Q3, and treated a speculative penalty strategy as a deterministic result in one scenario.
  • Primary cause: missing full-grid Q1/Q2 conversion and team/teammate fallbacks, not simply inaccurate front-runner pace. Those capabilities are now present in hierarchical_predict.py and will be used for Madrid.

Reliability update

Antonelli's Q3 lap receives a reduced Monza reliability weight of 0.5. Although he set 1:22.093 in Q3, his back-of-grid engine penalty and role in supporting Russell reduced the incentive for a normal final-lap programme. His faster 1:21.882 Q2 lap also shows that Q3 was not a clean expression of his maximum pace. Other clean Q3 laps retain 1.0 unless a documented issue is confirmed later.

The complete classification is stored in data/actual_qualifying.csv, Q3 times in data/qualifying_results.csv, reliability in data/weights.csv, and all stage-level and driver-level errors in the prediction evaluation CSVs.

reports.title: 2026 Zandvoort qualifying review
reports.html:
2026 Zandvoort qualifying review

The post-Friday forecast correctly predicted Norris, Russell, Antonelli, and Piastri in positions 1-4 and reduced position MAE from 2.000 to 0.500, so the Friday-stage weighting was successful. No permanent team-strength or driver-property score was changed from this single event: the McLaren and Mercedes teammate gaps were already accurately predicted, the Ferrari order was affected by late light rain and run timing, and Lawson's strong substitute performance needs another comparable sample. Only data reliability changed: Hamilton and Leclerc's Zandvoort weights moved from 1.0 to 0.7, Lawson's from 1.0 to 0.3, and Antonelli remains 0.5 because his 2025 baseline is a substituted Russell lap.

Wet or mixed forecast

This was conditional on qualifying being wet or mixed, not a forecast of rain occurrence. It used the post-Friday ranking as the car baseline and 200,000 simulations split evenly between mixed and fully wet conditions.

Mixed conditions applied 0.08s per score point with 0.25s random variation; fully wet conditions used 0.15s per point with 0.45s variation. These experimental probabilities had not yet been calibrated by backtesting.

Outcome

The post-Friday forecast correctly predicted the first four positions:

1Lando NorrisLando Norris

Across the eight drivers common to the forecast and actual classification, Friday evidence materially improved every ranking metric:

Forecast stageTime MAEPosition MAERank correlation
Pre-weekend0.334s2.0000.618
Post-Friday0.284s0.5000.929

Team conclusions

The actual Q3 team order was McLaren, Mercedes, Ferrari, then Red Bull. That is also the order implied by the post-Friday leading drivers, so no major permanent team-score rewrite is justified.

  • McLaren confirmed excellent Zandvoort pace. Norris beat Piastri by 0.142s; the forecast expected 0.130s. This is strong evidence that both the car ranking and their driver gap were well calibrated for this event.
  • Mercedes was only 0.102s from pole with Russell. Russell beat Antonelli by 0.031s; the forecast expected approximately 0.034s. The historical Mercedes track-fit assumption was directionally correct, although the original pre-weekend model overrated Antonelli because of his substituted 2025 baseline.
  • Ferrari was third among the four modeled front-running teams. Hamilton and Leclerc were separated by only 0.064s, but late light rain and run timing affected their final attempts. Their order must not update driver affinity.
  • Red Bull was fourth, with Verstappen 0.455s from pole. Lawson finished only 0.115s behind Verstappen despite joining Red Bull as a late substitute, much closer than the model expected. This is useful evidence that the car was better than Lawson's low-confidence forecast implied, but not enough to make a permanent Lawson skill change from one exceptional context.

Driver-score treatment

  • Norris, Russell, Antonelli, and Piastri require no immediate manual score change: their first-four order and both teammate gaps were predicted well.
  • Verstappen performed close to the post-Friday expectation relative to the event-wide time bias. His P7 is primarily evidence about current Red Bull dry pace, not a reason to reduce his wet or driver-skill score.
  • Hamilton and Leclerc receive no driver-score update from their Q3 ordering because the changing conditions made the comparison timing-dependent.
  • Lawson's result is flagged for future review, with no permanent score change until more same-team evidence exists.

Reliability decisions

  • Normal 1.0 Zandvoort reliability remains for clean comparable laps.
  • Antonelli remains 0.5 because his 2025 baseline is Russell's substituted Q3 time.
  • Hamilton and Leclerc are reduced to 0.7 because their final comparison was affected by late light rain and run order.
  • Lawson is reduced to 0.3 because his 2025 Racing Bulls and 2026 Red Bull laps are not a same-car year-over-year comparison and he entered as a late substitute.
